title: A word is sign plus bytes

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: A word is sign plus bytes

passages.title: A sign is not a sixth digit
passages.text:
A MIX word has five byte positions and a separate sign. Here b is the number of values a byte can hold, with 64 ≤ b ≤ 100. Byte d₁ is the most significant. Its contribution is d₁b⁴, whereas d₅ contributes only d₅. A MIX byte is not the modern eight-bit byte. In the formula, s is +1 or −1 for the separate sign, d_j is the digit in byte position j, and j runs from 1 to 5. The sum adds the five place-value contributions; it does not add the position labels.

Our main example encodes −130 in base 64. Two full groups of 64 and two remaining units occupy the last two compartments. Changing to b=100 changes the compartments to 1 and 30; the represented integer is still −130. A portable program must not assume that a single byte can contain 80.

passages.title: Equal values can have different representations
passages.text:
Positive zero and negative zero have identical byte magnitudes and different signs. Comparison treats them as equal, but a sign-sensitive load, multiplication, or conversion can preserve or reveal the distinction. Therefore storing only a language integer silently loses information.

The model retains a sign and five digits even when the magnitude is zero. The two-byte index registers are represented with three leading zero bytes; a value too large for their actual width is rejected rather than silently truncated.

passages.title: An address identifies a shelf
passages.text:
MIX has 4000 memory words, addressed 0 through 3999. A and X hold full words, I1 through I6 hold signed two-byte values, and J holds a nonnegative two-byte return address. Memory location 130 and the numeric value 130 are different kinds of thing. A load uses an address to find a word; an enter instruction uses an address field as a number.

The trace demonstrates representation, not a theorem that every Python integer fits in MIX. The width condition is essential: at base 64 a five-byte magnitude must be below 64⁵.

passages.title: Transfer the representation rule
passages.text:
When a sign is negative and every byte is zero, do not erase the sign. When the base changes, recompute positional digits instead of copying their labels. These two habits prevent different classes of emulator bugs: losing representation and confusing an integer with its encoding.

For a new example, 193 is 3·64+1, so its final bytes are 3 and 1. The same value in base 100 ends with 1 and 93. The bytes may differ while every integer calculation agrees.

title: Load and store selected fields

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.

passages.title: A field is an inclusive interval
passages.text:
Number the sign position 0 and bytes 1 through 5. A legal field L:R satisfies 0 ≤ L ≤ R ≤ 5. Its encoded F byte is 8L+R. Thus 2:4 is encoded by 20, not by 24. The interval selects adjacent positions, not a mask of unrelated bits. L names the first selected position and R the last, including both endpoints; F is the single byte that encodes that pair. For example, F=20 decodes to L=2 and R=4.

Loading selects the source field, right-aligns its bytes, and fills the remaining leading bytes with zeros. It takes the source sign only when L=0. A field excluding the sign loads a positive value even from a negative word.

passages.title: Store is not load backward
passages.text:
A store selects destination positions. It takes the required number of rightmost bytes from the register and inserts them into that destination interval. All unselected destination bytes survive. The sign changes exactly when position zero belongs to the field.

The main trace loads bytes 2 through 4 from a negative word, then places a register’s final two bytes into destination positions 1 and 2. The two operations align different objects; treating store as a reversed load would corrupt the untouched memory.
passages.formula: \text{destination}[L:R]\gets\text{rightmost register bytes of the required width}

passages.title: Sign-only fields expose the rule
passages.text:
Field 0:0 has no magnitude bytes. Loading it gives signed zero. Storing it changes only the destination sign. Field 1:5 copies all five magnitude bytes but deliberately leaves the sign out.

Index registers impose a second constraint: loading a field whose value needs more than two bytes is undefined in MIX. The interpreter reports that case before changing any register. A field can be syntactically legal and still be inappropriate for the chosen destination.

passages.title: Preservation is part of correctness
passages.text:
To verify a partial store, check every unselected byte, not merely the new field value. The independent tests cover all 21 legal intervals at several byte bases and both signs. Invalid intervals, such as 4:2, are rejected.

A new two-byte register value 5,6 stored into field 2:3 of a word 1,2,3,4,5 produces 1,5,6,4,5. The memory sign remains unchanged because the field starts after zero.

passages.title: Overflow is a persistent observation
passages.text:
For ADD and SUB, first compute the signed mathematical result. If its magnitude does not fit, retain its magnitude modulo b⁵ and turn overflow on. An ordinary nonoverflowing addition does not turn an already lit overflow indicator off. A result of numerical zero keeps A’s previous sign. V denotes the signed operand value obtained from the instruction’s selected memory field. W is one more than the largest five-byte magnitude; mod W keeps the remainder after removing complete groups of W.

This makes two kinds of state visible: a register value and a historical flag. The trace uses small, exact signed values before showing a boundary addition at the largest representable magnitude.

passages.title: A and X form a ten-byte magnitude
passages.text:
Multiplication places the high five bytes in A and low five in X. Both signs become the algebraic product sign, including when the product is zero. Division instead treats A:X as one ten-byte magnitude with A’s sign; X’s old sign is irrelevant. A:X means the magnitude formed by placing A’s five bytes before X’s five bytes. N is that full magnitude, q the quotient magnitude, and r the nonnegative remainder magnitude.

If V is nonzero and |A|<|V|, the quotient fits in A. Its sign is the quotient sign, while the remainder takes the old sign of A. If these conditions fail, MIX specifies undefined register information and overflow. Our model stops with an explicit undefined-state marker instead of inventing meaningful quotient bits.

passages.title: Shifts move bytes, comparisons select fields
passages.text:
SLA and SRA shift only A; SLAX and SRAX shift the concatenated ten bytes; SLC and SRC rotate those ten bytes. Signs are never shifted. A shift count is a byte count, so shifting by one is not multiplying by two. In the comparison formula, R means the selected register word and M the memory word; sign of their field difference returns less, equal, or greater.

CMP compares the same selected field in the register and memory. It does not compare an entire register to a right-aligned memory field. Its indicator is less, equal, or greater, and negative zero compares equal to positive zero.

passages.title: Know where the semantics stop
passages.text:
The executable interpreter includes integer arithmetic, all six shifts and all register comparison families. Floating-point modifier 0:6 is excluded. Index-register arithmetic must fit two bytes; unlike A arithmetic, an overflowing index calculation has no specified wrapped result.

A successful finite trace verifies this example, while the division identity explains all legal dividends. For a transfer case, 29 divided by −6 gives quotient −4 and remainder +5 when the dividend sign is positive.

title: Decode instructions and follow control

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: Fetch a word, then decode it
passages.text:
An instruction is a word whose first two bytes and sign encode an address, followed by an index selector I, modifier F, and opcode C. The fetch uses PC to read that word. Only then can execution determine what the fields mean. F is often a field interval, but for jumps and address transfers it selects a variant. PC is the program counter: the address of the instruction to fetch. The symbol ±AA is its signed address field, I selects an index register, and rI_I means that selected register’s contents. M is the resulting effective address or numeric operand, depending on the instruction.

Our trace executes an assembled loop, not a list of prewritten captions. Each next PC, memory access, flag, and clock value comes from decoding the fetched word.

passages.title: Default next and taken next differ
passages.text:
Ordinarily the next instruction is at P+1. A taken jump uses M instead, and normally saves P+1 in J. An untaken conditional jump leaves J unchanged. JSJ is the explicit exception: it jumps while preserving J. Here P is the value of PC before the instruction executes, so P+1 is the caller’s following instruction. J stores that continuation; M is the jump destination.

The index selector names a register; it is not itself the amount added. Thus address 120 indexed by register 1 containing −3 accesses location 117. Negative effective addresses can be valid numeric operands for ENTA but are invalid memory locations for LDA.
passages.formula: \text{taken ordinary jump}:\quad J\gets P+1,\quad PC\gets M

passages.title: Tests have their own state effects
passages.text:
JOV tests overflow and clears it if it was on; JNOV jumps when overflow is off and clears it if it was on. Consequently either instruction leaves overflow off. Comparison jumps leave the comparison indicator alone. Register-zero jumps treat either signed zero as zero. O names the overflow flag, and the subscript after means its value once the instruction has finished.

A single generic condition function is not enough if it omits these state effects. The test laboratory checks both outcomes of each overflow test and verifies J separately from PC.

passages.title: Reject before partially executing
passages.text:
The model validates memory addresses, index selectors, fields and supported modifiers. A diagnostic rolls the machine back to its preinstruction snapshot. This is a teaching guarantee for malformed encodings, not a claim that historical MIX defined every invalid program. S denotes the complete machine snapshot, including registers, flags, control, and memory; equality here requires every component to remain unchanged.

The difference matters when debugging: a failed load should not quietly advance PC and leave the learner inspecting a machine that never existed in the intended semantics.

passages.title: Issuing input does not finish input
passages.text:
IN starts a block transfer. If the same device is already busy, the instruction first waits for the prior operation. The newly started operation completes later. A program must not read its destination buffer while input is in progress. OUT has the dual obligation: do not modify its source buffer until output completes.

The executable scheduling model makes these states explicit. Its durations and block capacities are chosen teaching parameters, not measured MIX-device timings. The CPU and device can work simultaneously only on different owned data.

demonstration.title: Issuing input does not finish input

schedule.caption: Start: every buffer is EMPTY; no transfer or computation is active.
Issue input into EMPTY buffer 0; device busy until time 2.
CPU waits: no READY buffer exists yet.
Input completes into buffer 0; only now may the CPU read it.
CPU acquires oldest READY buffer 0; ownership prevents overwrite.
Input waits: backpressure leaves no EMPTY buffer.
Processing finishes; release buffer 0 for later input.
Issue input into EMPTY buffer 0; device busy until time 7.
CPU waits: no READY buffer exists yet.
Input completes into buffer 0; only now may the CPU read it.
CPU acquires oldest READY buffer 0; ownership prevents overwrite.

passages.title: Readiness tests and control operations
passages.text:
JBUS jumps while a device is busy; JRED jumps when ready. IOC waits for readiness and performs a device-specific operation such as a tape movement or printer page advance. Block sizes and allowed directions depend on the device, so a generic arbitrary-length read is not a complete MIX I/O model. In busy(d,t), d identifies the device, t is the current simulated time, and t_completion(d) is when its pending operation finishes.

Our integer instruction interpreter deliberately rejects opcodes 34–38. The separate scheduling model demonstrates readiness, ownership and waiting, without claiming tape positioning, disks, printer errors or a complete peripheral installation.

passages.title: Digits are characters before they are numbers
passages.text:
MIX character codes 30 through 39 encode decimal digits 0 through 9. CHAR writes ten decimal character bytes across A and X while preserving their signs. NUM reads each byte modulo ten to recover a decimal magnitude, preserves X and A’s sign, and can overflow A.

The code executes both conversions and tests their round trip for representable magnitudes. It does not pretend that the whole MIX character alphabet is ASCII or Unicode.

passages.title: Model time is not wall-clock time
passages.text:
MIX assigns relative instruction costs: ordinary loads, stores, additions, shifts and comparisons take 2u; multiplication and conversion take 10u; division takes 12u; MOVE takes (1+2F)u. Most other instructions take 1u, with waiting added where applicable. The letter u is one MIX time unit. In the cost sum, i identifies an instruction kind, f_i counts how often it executes, c_i is its cost per execution, and T_waiting is additional waiting time. Thus four additions at 2u each contribute 4×2u=8u.

The scheduling animation uses a separate chosen time scale. Neither Python execution duration nor animation speed is MIX execution time. A fast replay does not make an algorithm computationally cheaper.

title: Names become addresses

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: Labels name locations, not line numbers
passages.text:
An assembler tracks a location counter. A machine instruction or CON occupies one word and advances it. ORIG changes it, and EQU binds a symbolic value without reserving storage. A printed source-line number is merely an editing aid.

The example starts at 100. START therefore names location 100 even though preceding source lines exist. LOOP resolves to the address at which its instruction is emitted. No runtime instruction searches for the text LOOP.

passages.title: Resolve an instruction’s references
passages.text:
The assembler first discovers label locations, then translates instruction operands into numeric fields. A forward instruction reference can therefore point to a definition appearing later. Our restricted assembler accepts these forward A-part references; it does not implement every MIXAL future-reference rule or silently allocate misspelled names.

The emitted word is the machine program. Its listing keeps both the symbolic operand and numeric address so the learner can inspect the translation, rather than trusting an opaque compile button.

passages.title: Local labels are relative to source position
passages.text:
A definition such as 2H introduces a local occurrence. A reference 2B means the nearest preceding 2H; 2F means the nearest following one. Neither refers to the same line. This is a source-order rule, even if ORIG makes numeric addresses run backward.

The model resolves local references using source-row positions. Multiple definitions of a global name are rejected, while repeated local definitions are meaningful.

passages.title: Separate assembly from execution
passages.text:
ORIG 100 does not make the CPU jump to 100 when encountered at runtime: there is no ORIG instruction in the emitted memory. END supplies the starting address. EQU 4 does not load 4 into any register.

For a new source sequence ORIG 600; A CON 9; B HLT 0, A is 600 and B is 601. Inserting an EQU line between them changes neither address. Moving ORIG instead relocates subsequent emitted words, so every symbolic reference must be resolved against the new locations.

title: Build data and instructions with MIXAL

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: Build data and instructions with MIXAL

passages.title: One word can be built in pieces
passages.text:
CON can construct a word by placing values into specified fields. Each placement behaves like a store into an initially positive-zero word; a later overlapping placement replaces that part. This is useful for packed data and instruction-like records.

The main trace constructs a word with a signed address field and small control bytes. The result is calculated by the same field operations tested for machine stores, so the diagram and the numeric encoding agree.

passages.title: Expressions have a declared grammar
passages.text:
MIXAL expressions evaluate binary operations from left to right, rather than following ordinary multiplication precedence. For example, 2+3*4 means 20. Colon combines field endpoints as 8L+R. An asterisk used as an atom denotes the current location.

Our teaching assembler supports +, −, multiplication and colon, with explicit diagnostics for unsupported syntax. Full MIXAL also has division and scaled division; those operators and their signed-word subtleties are not implemented here.

passages.title: Literals create stored data
passages.text:
An operand such as =7= requests a constant word and uses its address. It is not an immediate add of seven. The restricted assembler puts literal words after the emitted source and includes them in memory. The program then fetches that constant exactly like any other data.

EQU, ORIG, CON and END are supported. ALF and the full character alphabet, punched-card formats, general W-value expressions and automatic allocation of undefined symbols are outside this assembler’s declared coverage.

passages.title: Inspect before running
passages.text:
Look at the location, sign, address bytes, index selector, F and C before treating the result as executable. An instruction word is data until fetched at PC; a data word may accidentally decode as an instruction if control falls into it. END and a terminating HLT keep the worked program’s control out of its data region.

A new field assignment 12(4:5) stores 12 in the least significant two-byte field. It does not mean decimal concatenation with the existing word.

passages.title: A complete original summation program
passages.text:
This program sums four signed words 7, −2, 9 and 4. A is the running total. I1 begins at −4, and the effective data address is DATA+4+I1. Each loop adds exactly one element, increments I1, and repeats while it is negative. TOTAL receives 18, then HLT stops before the data words.

The example is assembled and executed in the included model at byte bases 64, 73 and 100. These values and this program are original to the companion; no textbook program has been copied.

Original executable listing (label | operation | operand):

· | ORIG | 100

START | ENTA | 0

· | ENT1 | -4

LOOP | ADD | DATA+4,1

· | INC1 | 1

· | J1N | LOOP

· | STA | TOTAL

· | HLT | 0

DATA | CON | 7

· | CON | -2

· | CON | 9

· | CON | 4

TOTAL | CON | 0

· | END | START

passages.title: The invariant connects code to mathematics
passages.text:
Number additions from k=0. Before addition k, the first k elements have been summed and the next address is DATA+k. The ADD extends that prefix by one; INC1 makes the next index k+1−4. The branch repeats exactly when another element remains.

At exit I1=0, so four additions have occurred and A is the full sum. This argument assumes every partial sum fits a word. A different input can overflow even if its final mathematical sum is small.

passages.title: Count actual executions
passages.text:
The trace has two initialization instructions, four iterations of three instructions, a store and a halt: 16 executed instructions. With the declared MIX costs, the elapsed time is 1+1+4(2+1+1)+2+1=21u. Instruction count and elapsed MIX units are different measurements.

The final conditional branch is executed but not taken. Omitting it from a frequency count gives the wrong cost even though the final memory value remains right.

A new three-element input 5, −8, 6 has partial totals 5, −3, 3. Use the invariant to predict both A and I1, not only the final answer. The smaller help run actually assembles a two-element version.

title: Compose permutations and discover cycles

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: A permutation is a bijective renaming
passages.text:
A permutation p of {1,…,n} gives every object one image and every destination one preimage. Following images from an unvisited object must return to that starting object. It cannot first enter the middle of its path, because that would give one vertex two distinct preimages.

The model follows the arrows of an original six-element permutation and separates its disjoint cycles. Fixed points are cycles of length one and are retained when counting cycles.

passages.title: Declare composition order
passages.text:
We write p followed by q as p·q, following the source’s left-to-right convention. Thus (p·q)(i)=q(p(i)). Other texts use the opposite written order. The arrows remove the ambiguity: first follow p from i, then q from the intermediate object.

Composition is generally noncommutative. Testing one object whose images differ is enough to disprove equality of the two composed mappings.

passages.title: Cycles describe safe rearrangement
passages.text:
For a cycle (a b c), renaming sends a to b, b to c and c to a. If array contents are to move under that mapping, specify whether contents follow arrows or whether destination a reads old b. These conventions are inverses.

A temporary cell preserves the value that would otherwise be destroyed during a rotation. The directed graph explains why one temporary cell suffices per cycle and why separate cycles can be processed independently.

title: Invert a permutation without losing information

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

sections.title: Invert a permutation without losing information

passages.title: An inverse reverses every arrow
passages.text:
If p(i)=j, its inverse must satisfy p⁻¹(j)=i. A separate destination array makes this easy: write the index i at destination p(i). Doing the same writes into the original array is unsafe because a future successor may be overwritten before it is read.

Our original in-place variant follows one cycle, saves its next pointer in a temporary variable, then writes the predecessor with a negative tag. It is related to the source’s cycle-tagging idea but is not a copied implementation of either book algorithm.

passages.title: The saved successor justifies overwrite
passages.text:
During a cycle, current identifies the cell to replace, previous is its inverse image, and next is read from that cell before the write. Writing −previous cannot lose the onward path because next has already been saved. Cells tagged negative belong to completed reversed edges; untouched positive cells retain original successors.

Closing the cycle writes the final predecessor into the start cell. Only after all cycles are finished does a final pass remove negative tags.

passages.title: Tags need spare representation
passages.text:
Negative tags are safe because the input consists only of positive labels 1 through n. If arbitrary signed payloads were allowed, sign would no longer distinguish processed cells. This is an extra representation precondition, not a magic property of all arrays.

There are O(n) reads and writes and O(1) working scalars beyond the input. The displayed history uses extra storage for teaching replay, but that history is not workspace used by the inversion algorithm.

passages.title: Prove and test different things
passages.text:
The cycle invariant proves why every original edge is reversed without loss. Exhaustive tests through n=7 compare the output to the separate-array inverse, including fixed points and multiple cycles. Those tests detect implementation mistakes; they do not replace the invariant for arbitrary n.

A three-cycle 1→2→3→1 must become 1→3→2→1. Simply applying a[a[k]]=k from left to right can destroy this cycle’s information.

title: Relate cycles to records

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: Choose one cycle notation
passages.text:
Cycle notation can rotate each cycle and reorder different cycles without changing the permutation. To make it canonical, put the smallest element first in each cycle and order cycles by decreasing first element. Keep singleton cycles.

Now erase parentheses. The first item of every cycle is smaller than all earlier items, while no later item inside that cycle can be a new minimum. Thus cycle starts are precisely left-to-right minimum records.
passages.formula: i\text{ is a record}\iff i=1\text{ or }a_i<\min(a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1})

passages.title: The missing parentheses are recoverable
passages.text:
Scan the linear sequence and insert a left parenthesis before each new minimum. Close the preceding cycle there. This exactly reconstructs the canonical cycles, proving the transformation is reversible. The output linear sequence is generally a different one-line permutation from the original mapping.

The model shows original cycles, their canonical order, the erased sequence and the recovered breaks. It does not confuse a notation change with equality of the two one-line arrays.

passages.title: A bijection transfers a distribution
passages.text:
For a uniformly random permutation, the transformed linear sequence is also uniform because the transformation is one-to-one and onto. At position j, each of the first j elements is equally likely to be their minimum; hence that position is a record with probability 1/j. Linearity of expectation then gives expected cycle count Hₙ. C_n is the number of cycles in a permutation of n labels; E[C_n] means its average over all n! equally likely permutations. H_n is the harmonic sum 1+1/2+⋯+1/n.

Independence is unnecessary for this expectation calculation. The displayed finite example illustrates record positions, while symmetry and bijectivity establish the general statement.

title: Count fixed points with inclusion and exclusion

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: Count fixed points with inclusion and exclusion

passages.title: Fixed-point events overlap
passages.text:
Let Eᵢ be the event that a permutation fixes i. Subtracting all |Eᵢ| from n! removes a permutation with two fixed points twice. Inclusion–exclusion repairs such overlap by adding pair intersections, subtracting triple intersections, and continuing. D_n denotes the number of n-label permutations with no fixed point. The index k is the number of labels required to stay fixed in one correction; (−1)^k alternates addition and subtraction.

Fixing a chosen set of k labels leaves (n−k)! arrangements of the remaining labels. There are binomial(n,k) such sets. The model computes each signed correction for n=5 and the resulting derangement count 44.

passages.title: Check the coefficient of one permutation
passages.text:
A permutation with r fixed points appears in binomial(r,k) of the k-fold intersections. Its net coefficient is the alternating sum of these binomial coefficients. That sum is 1 when r=0 and 0 otherwise, so exactly the derangements survive.

This coefficient argument proves the formula without assuming that fixed-point events are independent. They are not independent in a finite permutation.

passages.title: Zero objects is a meaningful case
passages.text:
The empty permutation has no fixed points and is a derangement of an empty set, so D₀=1. One object cannot move elsewhere, so D₁=0. These cases make recurrences and counting identities work without an artificial exception.

To count permutations with exactly r fixed points, choose their labels and derange the rest. Choosing fixed points alone is insufficient because the remaining permutation must have no additional fixed points.

passages.title: An alternating correction is not a probability yet
passages.text:
Each displayed term is an integer count. Divide the final result by n! to obtain a probability. Intermediate alternating totals may temporarily overcount or undercount; they are not counts of a progressively filtered physical list.

For a new three-object case the corrections are 6−6+3−1=2. Exhaustive enumeration checks this and all sizes through seven; the coefficient proof covers every finite n.

scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: Call a routine and return safely

passages.title: A call needs a continuation
passages.text:
A call is more than a branch to useful code: the callee must know where to continue the caller. MIX’s ordinary jump saves the following address in J. Our original TWICE routine receives a number in A and returns twice that number in A. Its first instruction stores J into the address field of its return instruction.

The main program enters 11, calls TWICE, stores 22 and halts. The actual memory word containing the return jump is fetched after it has been changed; the model does not bypass self-modification with a hidden host-language return.

Original executable listing (label | operation | operand):

· | ORIG | 200

START | ENTA | 11

· | JMP | TWICE

· | STA | RESULT

· | HLT | 0

TWICE | STJ | RETURN

· | STA | TEMP

· | ADD | TEMP

RETURN | JSJ | 0

TEMP | CON | 0

RESULT | CON | 0

· | END | START

passages.title: Patch only the return address
passages.text:
STJ normally uses field 0:2. It writes J into the sign and two-byte address, preserving the return instruction’s index, modifier and opcode. The routine uses JSJ to return without overwriting J.

The trace displays the old and new return words. The proof obligation is spatial: only address positions change. If a full-word STJ were used accidentally, the jump opcode would be replaced by zero and the return would fail.

passages.title: State the entry and exit contract
passages.text:
Entry requires A=x, a valid caller continuation in J, writable TEMP and RETURN cells, and |2x|<b⁵. Exit returns A=2x and control to the caller’s continuation. TEMP and the return address field are clobbered; X and index registers are preserved.

The same patch cell cannot safely hold two simultaneous activations. Recursion, interrupts or a nested call using the same routine can overwrite an older continuation. A stack of activation records or another per-call storage convention is then required.

passages.title: Read the caller after the return
passages.text:
Successful arithmetic alone is not enough. The exit PC must equal the caller’s continuation, and promised preserved registers must still agree with entry. The tests check memory result 22, the preserved return opcode, and J=202.

For a transfer call with A=−6 the routine should return −12. If the caller needs its original A afterward, it must save it or request a different calling contract.

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.

sections.title: Measure reuse and specify side effects

passages.title: Reuse trades space for linkage
passages.text:
Suppose a body occupies B words and is used k times. Inlining copies B words at each site. A shared routine stores one body, an L-word linkage section, and C call-site words per use. Sharing saves space only when kB exceeds B+L+kC.

The computed example varies k while holding B=8, L=2, C=1. The threshold is an algebraic consequence of this declared design, not a universal property of all calling conventions.

passages.title: Time includes every entry and exit
passages.text:
If one execution of the useful body costs T and call/return overhead costs H, k inline uses cost kT, while shared execution costs k(T+H). Code size can improve while time worsens. Different hardware or compiler choices can change H.

In MIX, a simple jump, STJ and return already impose costs distinct from the routine’s arithmetic. Compare whole calling sequences, not only the instructions printed inside the body.

passages.title: Preservation is a resource decision
passages.text:
Saving registers adds time and temporary storage but can simplify callers. A contract should say which registers carry arguments and results, which are scratch, what memory is modified and which flags survive. An overflow flag can be a meaningful output even when A contains a wrapped value. The symbol π_preserved means “read only the fields promised unchanged.” The equation compares those fields at entry and exit, not the whole state or the changed result register.

The TWICE example promises X and index preservation but modifies A, TEMP, RETURN and J through the call. The computed preservation check compares entry and exit projections onto the promised state.

passages.title: Do not hide the activation model
passages.text:
A routine with one static return slot is economical for nonoverlapping calls but is not reentrant. A recursive routine needs distinct saved continuations and local storage for each live call. The memory cost is proportional to the number of simultaneous activations, not merely the number of source call sites.

The transfer check changes the number of call sites and asks when sharing first saves words. It also asks what must change before the same routine can call itself.

title: Resume where a coroutine paused

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: A paused computation keeps its place
passages.text:
A coroutine has a continuation and retained local state. Resuming it continues after its last yield rather than restarting at its entry. Our producer yields successive squares; its retained local counter names the next square to produce. The consumer has its own WAIT and USE locations.

The executable state machine records both continuation labels at every handoff. This is a semantic coroutine model, not a claim that a Python generator or a hardware thread executed invisibly.

passages.title: Save before transferring control
passages.text:
When the producer yields i², it saves ADVANCE as its next location. The consumer receives that one value and resumes USE. When control returns to the producer, it first increments the retained i; restarting at MAKE without advancing would repeat the same output.

MIX can encode continuations in writable jump-address fields. The source’s linkage idea motivates the model, but our square-stream state machine is original and separate from the integer instruction interpreter.

passages.title: Completion is another state
passages.text:
A coroutine may suspend repeatedly and then finish. The explicit END state distinguishes exhaustion from a legitimate yielded value such as zero. Resuming after END must not manufacture another item. P and C name the producer’s and consumer’s saved control locations. The counter i identifies the next square candidate, and n is the number of requested squares.

For n=0 the producer immediately reports completion. The consumer’s total stays zero, and no USE step occurs. Empty input is therefore handled by the same protocol rather than by an invented final payload.

passages.title: A coroutine is not automatically parallel
passages.text:
Only one component executes at each step in this model. Coroutines organize control cooperatively; simultaneous processors, data races and preemptive scheduling are different concerns. What survives suspension is precisely what the continuation contract retains.

For a new n=2 example, yields are 1 and 4. After the first yield, producer i is still 1 and its saved location is ADVANCE. Predicting those values tests continuation state, not just the final sum 5.

title: Join producer and consumer coroutines

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: Connect two stateful components
passages.text:
The producer emits squares 1² through n². The consumer adds each delivered value to a running total. A one-item handoff slot is either empty or contains a value awaiting consumption. Only the component owning that slot may change it. T_k is the consumer total after k items have been consumed; i is the square’s sequence index. For k=2, the equation reads T_2=1²+2²=5.

The trace includes yield, consume, resume and end events. Keeping the producer’s counter separate from the consumer’s total lets each component retain exactly the state needed for its own job.

passages.title: Exactly once is a protocol invariant
passages.text:
A successful yield fills the slot and moves the consumer to USE. USE adds the value once, empties the slot and moves back to WAIT. The producer cannot yield a second value before the first is consumed.

Consequently the number of consumed items never exceeds produced items, and their difference is zero or one. This makes duplicate consumption and overwritten values visible before a wrong final total appears.

passages.title: Exhaustion follows the final consumption
passages.text:
After consuming n², the consumer resumes the producer one more time. ADVANCE moves its counter beyond n, and MAKE then reports END. No extra square is yielded. This final control exchange is real work even though it adds no payload.

The result is checked against the independent closed form n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. That equality verifies the computed total, while the handoff invariant verifies its exactly-once construction.

passages.title: Change the stream without changing the contract
passages.text:
A producer could emit filtered values or decode variable-length records while the consumer kept the same one-item protocol. Both sides must still agree on whether END is separate from data, which side owns a pending item and what cancellation means.

This lesson models normal finite completion only; it does not implement asynchronous exceptions or cancellation. For n=3, the final total is 14 and exactly three USE events occur.

title: Programs can interpret other programs

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: The object program is data to the host
passages.text:
An interpreter keeps an object-language PC and dispatches object opcodes. The host program’s own control flow implements those operations. Our tiny stack language has PUSH, DUP, ADD and HALT. PUSH appends an integer; ADD removes two integers and pushes their sum. In the state formula, pc is the object program’s next instruction position and σ is its stack sequence, written from bottom to top. The symbol ‖ appends a sequence: σ‖[v] adds v at the top. The labeled arrow denotes one executed object instruction.

The original object program pushes 4, duplicates it, adds the pair, pushes 3, adds again and halts. The result 11 arises from actual dispatch, with the object stack recorded after each instruction.

passages.title: One object step can require many host steps
passages.text:
Fetching an opcode, validating its operands, checking stack depth and updating the stack are host actions. They collectively implement one object instruction. Counting host statements as object instructions mixes two levels of explanation. The displayed tail [a,b] has a below b on the stack. ADD removes both, computes a+b, and appends that one sum to the untouched older stack σ.

Each computed frame identifies fetch, dispatch and update as distinct host responsibilities and records the resulting object state after one object step. It does not claim to show a separate executed host instruction for each diagram box. The object PC advances once, and the displayed stack contains no accidental host temporaries.

passages.title: A language needs failure rules
passages.text:
ADD requires at least two stack entries, DUP at least one, and every fetched opcode must be supported. An invalid program produces a diagnostic. The model does not silently treat unknown instructions as no-ops.

HALT is an explicit instruction. Reaching beyond the code array is not implicitly successful termination; that would hide missing branches or forgotten halts.

passages.title: Compact representation is a design choice
passages.text:
An object language can package repeated complex host behavior into short codes. Porting then requires another implementation of the object semantics, not a rewrite of every object program. The advantage depends on instruction design and dispatch overhead; interpretation is not inherently slower or faster in every setting.

For transfer, PUSH 6; DUP; ADD leaves 12. Removing DUP causes stack underflow, demonstrating that the intermediate state matters as much as the intended arithmetic.
passages.formula: \text{object semantics is the contract between code and interpreter}

title: Build a faithful integer MIX subset

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: A faithful subset starts with explicit state
passages.text:
The integer MIX model stores 4000 addressable words, A and X, six narrow index registers, J, PC, overflow, comparison and simulated time. Words retain sign separately from magnitude. One step fetches the memory word currently at PC, including any self-modification by earlier stores. In S, M is memory, O is overflow, C is the comparison indicator, and t is guest elapsed time. I_1 through I_6 are index-register contents; they are distinct from an instruction’s index selector.

The title’s goal is fidelity to the supported subset, not a claim of a complete MIX installation. The executed examples and the declared diagnostics define what this implementation can demonstrate.

check.prompt: Why must a fetched MIX word come from current guest memory?
choices: Host code knows the intended opcode
An earlier store may have modified the instruction
check.explanation: Self-modifying return code changes an instruction’s address field. Fetching stale original source would bypass actual guest semantics.

passages.title: The implemented instruction families
passages.text:
The interpreter implements NOP and HLT; integer ADD, SUB, MUL and DIV; all positive/negative loads; stores including STJ and STZ; address transfers; comparisons; comparison, overflow and register jumps; six shifts; sequential MOVE; NUM and CHAR. Each family decodes its own F meaning.

Floating-point operations and I/O opcodes 34–38 are excluded from this interpreter. I/O readiness and buffering are implemented in a separate parameterized scheduling model. The assembler is also a stated MIXAL subset, not a full language implementation.

passages.title: Undefined behavior is not a guessed value
passages.text:
An invalid address, malformed field, unsupported instruction or index overflow produces a transactional diagnostic. Division by zero or an oversized quotient instead sets overflow and reaches an explicit undefined-result stop, matching the fact that MIX does not specify meaningful A and X bits afterward.

The preserved predivision register bits are available only as diagnostic context; they must not be read as the division result. Distinguishing these cases is more honest than inventing a wrapped quotient.

passages.title: Simulated cost belongs to the guest
passages.text:
The CLOCK field advances by documented MIX units for executed instructions. Browser animation duration, Python runtime and host loop iterations are not included. Device waiting has its own explicit model and cannot be inferred from these CPU-only program timings.

The trace of the original four-element sum reaches TOTAL=18 in 21u at every tested byte base. That portability check verifies these programs; it does not prove every arbitrary word-level program is base-independent.

title: Test a simulator at its semantic edges

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: Test a simulator at its semantic edges

passages.title: Test representations, not only values
passages.text:
An assertion that A equals zero misses whether its sign is correct. A field test that checks selected bytes but ignores untouched bytes misses corruption. The laboratory therefore compares signed digit arrays, flags, J, PC and changed memory as well as numerical results.

Its independent field oracle uses positional sums and position-wise expected stores, rather than calling the implementation’s field helper again. This gives a genuinely different path to the expected answer.

passages.title: Boundary cases make hidden rules visible
passages.text:
The tests include all 21 valid fields, both signs, multiple byte bases, ±0, conversion round trips, taken and untaken overflow jumps, division failure, invalid addressing and sequential overlapping MOVE. These cases target places where a superficially plausible emulator can disagree with the specification.

For example, copying an overlapping MOVE through a temporary slice produces a different result from MIX’s one-word-at-a-time movement. The source word can propagate into several destinations.

passages.title: An invalid instruction must not half-run
passages.text:
Our diagnostic contract says that rejected instructions leave the whole state unchanged. Tests snapshot PC, registers, flags and memory before a bad instruction and compare afterward. This catches a common bug: incrementing PC before validation and forgetting to roll it back.

This extra diagnostic discipline is a model design choice. It is distinguished from legal MIX semantics and from hardware behavior on undefined input.

title: Trace without changing the program's meaning

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: Trace without changing the program's meaning

passages.title: Observe snapshots without executing twice
passages.text:
A trace should record what the program did, not repeat its instructions in order to discover their effects. Our observer copies state after each committed step. The unobserved baseline runs the same program without retaining those copies; their guest results must agree. The symbol π_guest means “keep only the guest machine fields being compared.” S_traced and S_baseline are the two complete run snapshots; the observer’s separate log is omitted by that projection.

The demonstration pairs guest snapshots and a separate event log. Logging a memory store is safe only because the observer copies the resulting state; reissuing the store or output operation would change the program.

passages.title: Keep observer storage separate
passages.text:
A guest program may write any permitted guest memory location. Putting trace records into that same address space without a reservation can overwrite code or data. Our logs live in host-side storage and are absent from guest memory.

An in-machine tracing routine would need a stronger calling contract: save and restore registers and flags, use disjoint memory, and intercept control transfers correctly. That machinery is discussed conceptually here, not falsely claimed as an implemented MIX trace routine.
passages.formula: M_{\rm guest}\cap M_{\rm observer}=\varnothing\quad\text{in the host-side design}

passages.title: Decide what equivalence observes
passages.text:
The CPU-only examples compare registers, flags, guest memory, halted status and guest CLOCK. Host elapsed time and log size differ. If guest behavior depended on real-time devices, instrumentation could affect when a readiness test succeeds; semantic equivalence would then need a carefully controlled device-time model. This displayed tuple defines exactly what π reads: registers, control, flags, memory, halt status and guest time. Equality means equality of these fields individually.

Thus our equality claim is scoped to deterministic CPU programs with the same initial state and documented guest timing.

passages.title: A trace explains a branch after it happens
passages.text:
The trace records the fetched word, effective address, cost and whether the branch was taken. It does not infer a jump merely from a changed PC, since a jump can target the sequential next address. It also distinguishes a taken JSJ from a jump that updates J. In the event tuple, I is the fetched instruction word, M its effective address, taken says whether its branch was followed, and S_after is the committed resulting snapshot.

For transfer, adding an observer log entry may change host runtime and storage use. It should not change the computed total or execute an output twice.

title: Overlap useful work with input

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: Two buffers let different jobs overlap
passages.text:
With one buffer, input fills it, the CPU processes it, and only then may input reuse it. With two buffers, input can fill one while the CPU processes the other. The ownership condition is essential: they cannot safely work on the same data simultaneously. In the formula, n is the number of items, I is input time per item, C is processing time per item, T_1 is total time with one buffer, and T_2 with two. Here n=4, I=3, C=5: T_1=32 and T_2=3+5+3×5=23.

The event model uses four input items, input time 3 and processing time 5. It shows startup, simultaneous work, waits and final drain, rather than drawing two idealized bars that omit boundary costs.

passages.title: A completion event changes permission
passages.text:
Issuing input changes EMPTY to FILLING. Only its completion changes FILLING to READY. The CPU acquires the oldest READY buffer and changes it to PROCESSING. Its completion returns the buffer to EMPTY.

At equal timestamps, completed input and computation are recognized before new work is issued. This explicit event ordering makes the zero-wait handoff deterministic without allowing premature reads.
passages.formula: \mathrm{CPU\ may\ read}\iff\mathrm{state}=\mathrm{READY\ or\ PROCESSING\ owned\ by\ CPU}

passages.title: Startup and drain cannot be hidden
passages.text:
For four items with I=3 and C=5, serial time is 32 while two-buffer time is 23. The first input still costs 3 before computation begins, and the last computation still needs its full service time after its input arrives.

The formula assumes one serial input device, one serial processor, constant positive service times, instantaneous handoffs and enough buffers. It is not a prediction for arbitrary disks, operating systems or variable workloads.

passages.title: Know when to stop reading
passages.text:
The model receives a known item count and never issues a read beyond it. Other protocols require an explicit end marker or a short-block convention; speculative read-ahead must respect whichever protocol applies. An empty stream takes no service time.

For a new two-item case with I=4 and C=2, two-buffer time is 4+2+4=10, not 8. The limiting input rate does not eliminate the final processing drain.

title: Manage multiple buffers as a queue

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

sections.title: Manage multiple buffers as a queue

passages.title: Buffers are owned resources
passages.text:
A pool of k buffers is partitioned among EMPTY, FILLING, READY and PROCESSING states. Each buffer has exactly one state and at most one active owner. A READY queue records arrival order. The CPU removes its oldest entry; input chooses only an EMPTY buffer. E, F, R and P count buffers in the four named states; k counts all buffers. These are counts, not buffer identities: moving one buffer from FILLING to READY decreases F by one and increases R by one.

The animation gives each physical buffer a stable identity as its state changes, so reuse cannot be confused with creating a new buffer.

passages.title: Backpressure prevents overwrite
passages.text:
If the producer finishes faster than the consumer, READY buffers accumulate. Eventually no EMPTY buffer remains, and input must wait. This is backpressure, not a bug. If input is slower, the CPU waits because there is no READY item.

The computed three-buffer example shows both queue membership and explicit busy or waiting status. A state change is justified by completion or acquisition, never by an arbitrary animation timer.

passages.title: More storage does not remove a bottleneck
passages.text:
Extra buffers can absorb short-term variation but cannot make one serial processor consume faster than its service time, or one device produce faster than its service time. For constant service times, two buffers already achieve the steady-state bottleneck rate in this model. I is the input service time per item and C the processing service time per item. Throughput counts completed items per time unit, so its limiting rate is the smaller of 1/I and 1/C.

The demonstration compares one, two and three buffers using the same workload. It reports total completion times including startup and drain, not only an asymptotic rate.

passages.title: FIFO is a separate invariant
passages.text:
Exclusive ownership prevents races but does not itself guarantee data order. The READY queue carries that second responsibility. Tests verify that the output identifiers are exactly 0,1,…,n−1, with no missing, repeated or reordered item.

A multi-device shared pool needs further policies to avoid one device monopolizing every empty buffer. This model has one producer and one consumer; it does not claim a general deadlock-free multi-device allocator.

title: Format variable output incrementally

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanations, inputs, diagrams, assessments and executable models after the cited concepts. No source programs, textbook prose, page images or private source files are included.
scope: Four operation-focused demonstrations with separately computed smaller examples. Integer MIX and MIXAL have explicit supported subsets; coroutine, interpreter and device-scheduling models are named abstractions. Finite checks are implementation evidence, not proofs of all inputs.

passages.title: Logical records need not fit physical blocks
passages.text:
Logical records can have different lengths, while a device may require fixed-capacity physical blocks. Packing follows the concatenated payload stream, filling each block and carrying a record’s remaining characters into the next. Record boundaries need separate information if they must later be reconstructed. Each r_i is one logical record, m is the number of records, and ‖ means concatenate their characters in order. Record identity is retained separately in the length list.

Our original records AB, CDEFG and H have lengths 2,5,1. With capacity five, the physical payloads become ABCDE and FGH. The model retains record lengths [2,5,1] as metadata.

passages.title: The cursor identifies the next free position
passages.text:
Appending a character increases the fill count. When it reaches capacity, the block is emitted and the cursor returns to zero. A record boundary alone does not force a flush under this policy. The cursor c counts characters already consumed. Input[0:c] means the prefix starting at position zero and stopping just before c; ‖ joins the emitted and still-pending character sequences.

The invariant is that emitted valid payloads followed by the pending buffer equal exactly the already consumed input prefix. It proves neither duplication nor omission occurs when a record crosses a block boundary.

choices: Keep a full pending block indefinitely
Emit AB and reset the cursor
check.explanation: The append reaches capacity exactly, so a full block is emitted and the next free position returns to zero.

passages.title: A partial final block needs its valid length
passages.text:
At end of input, a nonempty pending block is flushed with its valid payload length. Any physical padding is outside that length and is not logical data. An exactly full final block has already been emitted and must not produce an extra empty block. N is the total number of payload characters and B the physical block capacity. The ceiling brackets round N/B up to the next whole block; for N=8 and B=5, two blocks are needed.

An empty stream produces no blocks. Empty records still require their zero lengths in the record metadata if record identity matters; they cannot be recovered by examining payload alone.

passages.title: Reconstruction checks the whole contract
passages.text:
Concatenate valid block payloads, then split at the cumulative record lengths. This recovers both payload and original records. A sentinel-based alternative would require escaping the sentinel when it appears in data; this lesson deliberately uses lengths instead.

For transfer, records XYZ and PQ packed into capacity three produce XYZ and PQ, with final valid length two. Changing capacity changes physical grouping, not the logical stream.
